en: The *Vilomākṣara-Rāmakṛṣṇa-kāvya* (The Poem on Rāma and Kṛṣṇa with Reversed Syllables)
I bow to that son of the Earth (Buddha), whose liberation is a noble smile, from whom the glory of compassion arises for those capable of liberation;
to the illustrious Yādava (Kṛṣṇa), who is like a cloud for the crops of the capable, and whose liberation is the cessation of the life-force of Mura. || 1 ||
For a long time she was Brahmā, yet not for long was she Brahmā; she is that which possesses form, whose stars are true and existent.
She is that which possesses form, whose stars are true and existent; for a long time she was Brahmā, yet not for long was she Brahmā. || 2 ||
In that which is unreal, there is the boundary of reality; it is called "dark" (tāmasī) as it acts through illusion (māyā), being incapable of enduring and yet appearing before the eyes.
It is like an illusion that is both imperishable and present before the senses; it is called "dark" in that which is unreal, for it possesses the limit of reality.
That which destroys affliction, beginning with the stars, is sinless; the threefold knowledge is not for the purpose of heat in one's dwelling.
Service is constant; it is not to be undertaken by Kṛṣṇa. For the Creator, it is the banner that destroys the nature of ignorance and sin.
From Śrīrāma, by whom the wise one is constantly led from the middle way through the power of Vaśyavatī,
may the immortal Śrī lead him from here toward Dvārāvatī, which is under the control of Vaśya, along the middle path.

O Kauśikī, you who practiced the triple asceticism and observed the vow of dripping [the sacrificial offering], you gave away the two sons of your distressed mother; O bird-haired one, you who know that [deed], you have now come to this fierce forest to sport.

O you with long lips and thighs, go, go to the place where the three take refuge; O you who have received the command, protect the one who has come to the perishable! You who have known the scriptures, go indeed; for that army and force which obstructed the Child—go against them! || 7 ||

The daughter of the ocean, whose course is eternal, who flows toward the white shore, and who resembles a boat being propelled by her [the wind]—surely she, like the full moon, having come to the lowest ebb, has carried away his life. || 8 ||
Those who were born from the depths of the sacrifice and are considered by the Rākṣasa to have passed away,
they have gone beyond the darkness and the imperishable, having reached the goal through their cries.
Compassion toward the gods should exist only as long as there is no latent impression;
the deity of the Yādava lineage is not to be sung in the Veda with wine or without compassion.
In the assembly halls, his bow was shattered by this one who, with a wrath like that of the God of Death, [struck] with stone-tipped shafts;
he whose thunderbolt-like arms were obstructed by mountain peaks, and in whom fear was submerged within his own splendor amidst the five-faced [Śiva].
Who knows that Sītā who shines as the imperishable syllable? What star is there for one conquered by Viṣṇu in debate?
What is the state of change for one protected by the gods? That boundary was maintained by the descendant of Yadu through his forbearance.
The noble one of the Tīvragaurava lineage was esteemed by the mind of Vaidehī;
he did not practice the vow of the cow for the sake of worldly travel, nor was he overcome by darkness, O lords of the earth.
She who dwells in the lotus and descended with Rādhā— O Nanda, that Rādhā of yours is now at the home of the Yādava.
O King, he who was the festival among the gods, who was not obstructed in his slaying of Śiva’s followers,
and who was the wise Vatsapa among men according to the Veda, has been slain by this one while they were helpless.
O you who go to protect the Nagas, let my Pinaka bow be discharged; O Unborn One, grant me the gift of the wealth of Dharma.
O you whose face is joy, in the wealth of Dharma there is victory; by whomsoever I am protected, you are our protector. 16.
The beautiful-eyed woman stretched a garland for her own feet;
she did not consider her own beauty as lovely as that which she obtained from the garland when she bowed down. 17.
May this curse of mine depart from her;
may she be freed from the fear of the serpent-demon, and may she be measured as the most excellent among those who have transcended all bonds.
I am not one who dispels shame through the knowledge of faults; I am steadfast, smiling today with no reproach.
I am a renouncer through wisdom, devoted to truth; I am humble, ignorant, and my path ends at the feet of the worthy.
The monk Yātādhirāpa, of the stainless Jāva lineage, entered the house of Sambhāvita;
there he slew Śava, who had been agitated by passion for his own transgression and was shining with splendor.

O Pināka-bearer, let not that twofold public scandal reach you through her excessively loud voice—that which someone else obtained when the time for the sound of the elephant-riders' departure had passed. (21)
Upon the corpse, the variegated deer-patterned cloth did not please her; nor did the five-fold laughter of the jesters.
Like a dancing girl moving through the wind, she entered a certain house of ill repute.
O you who are intoxicated by your own views, do you not cast down your own neck here, for you grieve that Mālinī?
O best among the Yadus, you cast down the blue-necked one who honors you upon his vehicle, the bird-bearer.

May he who, while wandering at the edge of the forest, felt no aversion toward a woman in the wilderness despite her subtle pains; he who is steadfast, whose delight is immeasurable, and who has extended for you the illusory resonance of the flute through his beautiful voice—may he protect you. (24)

Why indeed is Pampā, whose waters are so delicious, not resorted to by one who is self-restrained? Or what sin does it fail to wash away for one who dwells there, as it were, in the abode of Vainateya?

He, who removes the heat of those who bow before him, extended his own protection over that man who had committed no offense against him; he led him away from this world to the destruction of his enemies.

Through the division of the *kapitāla* [meter], that woman is won over by conciliation; indeed, in that conduct, he is one who brings about the future flowering of the creeper upon the mountain of faults. || 27 ||

Those rows of peacocks in the assembly hall, fashioned like clouds with their slightly spreading plumage, shine like a dark ocean of bees, appearing as if they were the very essence of the cuckoo’s brilliance.
When Rāvaṇa bowed down out of shame at being struck by the arrow, his head did not undergo even a slight, unsteady whirling;
rather, that bowing of the bird-like head was a worthy vessel for the cloud-like [arrow] to descend upon him for the sake of sport.
In the divine yoga, there is service and giving; there is no doubt regarding the journey to Laṅkā.
One should not go at an improper time, by which the sky is reached; it is to be sung with the Vedas in the abode of Nanda.
In traveling by carriage, on a river, in battle, in a garden, or in leading [others], there is room for doubt, contempt, permission, and opportunity;
in traveling by carriage, on a river, in battle, in a garden, or in leading [others], there is room for doubt, contempt, permission, and opportunity. || 31 ||
Or he assigned him to the task of building a bridge across the two-fold ocean,
so that by means of reeds, he might become a leader who guides others with clarity during the day.
"Vāyu is permitted [as our ally], but not Aravita; on this day in battle, we shall cease from fire.
Therefore, the youth considered his meal. (33)

Wherein that long-eyed one, for the sake of the wounded Raghu, led away those whose lives were spent, who followed him as attendants, who were of different ages and various paths, and who resembled wild forest trees— having joined with the three terrible enemies.
In the city of Śrīpura, the enemy of Tāraka, accompanied by the daughter of Dāsa, attained splendor; for who among beautiful women would not always delight in virtuous conduct? 35.
Lanka, which is the superimposition of the limbs of the poor man, is to be measured within the expanse of the vehicle;
the full moon night is to be served during the watch, leading one through time in the form of the glow of twilight.
Thus ends the *Vilomākṣara-Rāmakṛṣṇa-kāvya*, composed by the illustrious astrologer-poet Sūryakavi.
